Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

derivations.claim: (Quadratic remainder around the flat metric.) Let $A_{ab}(\varepsilon):=g_{ab}(\varepsilon)-\eta_{ab}$. By [L2], $\sup_K|A|\le C'\varepsilon$, $L^{-1}\sup_K|\partial A|\le C'\varepsilon$ and $L^{-2}\sup_K|\partial^2A|\le C'\varepsilon$ for $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$; shrinking the threshold if necessary so that the quantity in [L1] is at most $\delta_0$, [L1] gives at once $$|G_{ab}(g(\varepsilon))-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A(\varepsilon))|\le C_2\varepsilon^2/L^2$$ for a constant $C_2$ depending only on $C,L$. This is (a).

(The diagonal perturbation.) Put $h_{ab}$ for the component field with $h_{00}=-2\varphi$, $h_{ij}=-2\varphi\delta_{ij}$ and $h_{0i}=0$, so that $A(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon h+s(\varepsilon)$ with $s(\varepsilon)_{00}=r_{00}$, $s(\varepsilon)_{ij}=r_{ij}$, $s(\varepsilon)_{0i}=r_{0i}$. For $h$: the trace is $h=\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=2\varphi-6\varphi=-4\varphi$, and $\bar h_{ab}=h_{ab}-\tfrac12h\eta_{ab}$ gives $\bar h_{00}=-2\varphi-\tfrac12(-4\varphi)(-1)=-4\varphi$ and $\bar h_{ij}=-2\varphi\delta_{ij}+2\varphi\delta_{ij}=0$, while $\bar h_{0i}=0$. Substituting in the formula of [L1]: $G^{(1)}_{00}(h)=-\tfrac12\Box\bar h_{00}-\tfrac12\eta_{00}\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}=2\Box\varphi+\tfrac12\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}$; the last term is $\eta^{00}\eta^{00}\partial_0\partial_0\bar h_{00}=0$ by stationarity [L3], and $\Box\varphi=(-c^{-2}\partial_t^2+\Delta)\varphi=\Delta\varphi$ because $\partial_0\varphi=0$ with $\partial_t=c\partial_0$. Hence $G^{(1)}_{00}(h)=2\Delta\varphi$. For the spatial components all terms vanish: $\bar h_{ij}=0$, the divergence terms $\partial^c\partial_{(i}\bar h_{j)c}$ involve only $\bar h_{00}$ differentiated in $x^0$ and hence vanish by stationarity, and $\bar h_{0i}=0$ gives $G^{(1)}_{0i}(h)=0$.

(Split of the perturbation.) By linearity of $G^{(1)}$ in [L1], $G^{(1)}(A(\varepsilon))=\varepsilon G^{(1)}(h)+G^{(1)}(s(\varepsilon))$; combined with step 1.1 this gives $$G_{ab}(g(\varepsilon))=\varepsilon G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)+G^{(1)}_{ab}(s(\varepsilon))+O(\varepsilon^2/L^2)$$ with the bound of step 1.1.

(Bounds for the remainder term.) From [L2], $|s_{00}|+|s_{ij}|\le C\varepsilon^2$, $L|\partial s_{00}|+L|\partial s_{ij}|\le C\varepsilon^2$ and $|s_{0i}|,L|\partial s_{0i}|,L^2|\partial^2s_{0i}|\le C\varepsilon^{3/2}$, and only second derivatives of $s$ occur in the formula of [L1]. Hence $|G^{(1)}_{ij}(s)|\le C\varepsilon^2/L^2$ and $|G^{(1)}_{0i}(s)|\le C\varepsilon^{3/2}/L^2$. Moreover the $s_{0i}$-terms do not contribute to the $00$-component: in the formula of [L1] the $\bar s_{0i}$ enter the $00$-component only through $\partial^c\partial_{(0}\bar s_{0)c}=\partial^c\partial_0\bar s_{0c}$, which vanishes because $\partial_0s=0$ by [L3], and through $\partial^c\partial^d\bar s_{cd}$, in which the mixed coefficients $\eta^{0i}$ vanish; the remaining $s_{00},s_{ij}$ terms are $O(\varepsilon^2/L^2)$. Consequently $|G^{(1)}_{00}(s)|\le C\varepsilon^2/L^2$.

(Component hierarchy of the Einstein tensor.) Combining steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1: $G_{00}(g(\varepsilon))=2\varepsilon\Delta\varphi+O(\varepsilon^2/L^2)$, and $2\varepsilon\Delta\varphi=2\Delta(\varepsilon c^2\varphi)/c^2=2\Delta\Phi/c^2$; further $|G_{ij}|\le C\varepsilon^2/L^2$ and $|G_{0i}|\le C\varepsilon^{3/2}/L^2$. This is (b).

(Stress-energy hierarchy and the Poisson equation.) Since $G=\kappa T$ by [L4], dividing by $\kappa$ gives the three bounds of (c). For the Poisson equation, the first bound reads $\kappa T_{00}=2\Delta\Phi/c^2+O(\varepsilon^2/L^2)$; writing $T_{00}=\rho_\varepsilon c^2+\eta_\varepsilon$ with $|\eta_\varepsilon|\le C\varepsilon^2c^4/(G_NL^2)$, the left-hand side is $\kappa\rho_\varepsilon c^2+\kappa\eta_\varepsilon=(8\pi G_N/c^2)\rho_\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2/L^2)$ because $\kappa c^4/(G_NL^2)=8\pi/L^2$; multiplying the resulting inequality by $c^2/2$ gives $|\Delta\Phi-4\pi G_N\rho_\varepsilon|\le C_2\varepsilon^2c^2/L^2$.

(Scaled form and conclusion.) On the scaled region, $\Delta_X\psi(X)=L^2\Delta\varphi(LX)$ and $4\pi R(X)=4\pi G_NL^2\rho_\varepsilon(LX)/(\varepsilon c^2)$; multiplying the Poisson inequality of step 5.1 evaluated at $LX$ by $L^2/(\varepsilon c^2)$ gives $|\Delta_X\psi-4\pi R|\le C_2\varepsilon$, which is (d). Steps 1.1, 4.1 and 5.1 give (a), (b) and (c); all thresholds and constants depend only on $C$, $L$ and the dimension.

step 1.2 computes the exact first-order coefficient G^(1) of the diagonal perturbation h and step 4.1 shows the leading term of G_{00} is 2εΔφ; the zero case of the linearized perturbation s(ε) is the case treated exactly in step 1.2.

The theorem states component inequalities and a conditional Poisson estimate, not an equivalence.
No converse (for example that every prescribed density admits such data) is asserted; the existence of the family is a hypothesis.

$\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$ as in the framework's convention. All components below
are taken in the inertial chart, and $\partial_a$ are the chart derivatives.

**(a) Structural data.** A tuple $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ is
**stationary weak-field data** when

- $K\subseteq\Omega$ is a compact set, $L>0$, $C>0$ and
  $\varepsilon_0>0$ are constants;
- $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth dimensionless function and
  $r=(r_{ab})$ is a family of component functions
  $r_{ab}(\varepsilon,p)$, defined for $\varepsilon\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
  and $p\in\Omega$ for some $\varepsilon_1>\varepsilon_0$ and smooth in
  $(\varepsilon,p)$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]);
- for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\varepsilon,p)=\begin{cases}-(1+2\varepsilon\varphi(p))+r_{00}(\varepsilon,p),&a=b=0,\\[2pt] r_{0i}(\varepsilon,p),&\{a,b\}=\{0,i\},\\[2pt] (1-2\varepsilon\varphi(p))\,\delta_{ij}+r_{ij}(\varepsilon,p),&a=i,\ b=j,\end{cases}$$

  is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\varepsilon)$ on
  $\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]);
- **(stationarity)** $\partial_0\varphi=0$ and $\partial_0r_{ab}=0$ on
  $\Omega$ for all $a,b$ and all $\varepsilon$, so that
  $\partial_0g_{ab}(\varepsilon,\cdot)=0$;
- **(bounds)** for every multiindex $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le2$ and every
  $p\in K$,

$$|\partial^\alpha\varphi(p)|\le\frac{C}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{00}(\varepsilon,p)|+|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}(\varepsilon,p)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^2}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{0i}(\varepsilon,p)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L^{|\alpha|}} .$$

  (Here $|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}|$ stands for the maximum over $i,j$ and
  $|\partial^\alpha r_{0i}|$ for the maximum over $i$.)

**(b) Derived data.** For stationary weak-field data define the
**potential**

$$\Phi:=\varepsilon c^2\varphi\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$

a smooth stationary function of dimension $\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-2}$ in
the framework's unit conventions. The symmetric component family
$g(\varepsilon)-\eta$ is the **perturbation of the family**.

**(c) Einstein families.** Stationary weak-field data form an **Einstein
family with coupling $\kappa$** when for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$
there is a smooth symmetric component field $T_{ab}(\varepsilon,\cdot)$ on
$\Omega$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) satisfying

$$G_{ab}\bigl(g(\varepsilon)\bigr)=\kappa\,T_{ab}(\varepsilon)\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$

where $G$ is the Einstein tensor of the metric-selected connection of
$g(\varepsilon)$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). In that case define the
**density read from the time-time component**

$$\rho_\varepsilon:=\frac{T_{00}(\varepsilon)}{c^2}\qquad\text{on }\Omega .$$

**(d) Scope.** This item fixes a class of metric families and the vocabulary
of the weak-field bridge: the component form, the stationarity of the data,
the derivative bounds, the potential, and the equation that upgrades the
data to an Einstein family. It asserts that no family exists, that
$\partial_0$ is a Killing field or timelike, that the inverse metrics are
uniformly bounded or that the density is positive; those are consequences
proved separately where they are used. The family is an explicit
input-family hypothesis: neither its existence for prescribed Newtonian
initial data nor its construction from other data is claimed. The physical
reading of the components, of $G_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$, of $\Phi$ and of
$\rho_\varepsilon$ belongs to the framework's postulates and unit
conventions, which are separate items.

Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data
over an open set $\Omega$ of the flat model
([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]], [[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]]),
and let $E(\varepsilon):=g(\varepsilon)-\eta$ and
$H(\varepsilon):=\eta^{-1}E(\varepsilon)$ be the component matrices of the
perturbation and of its $\eta$-raise. Let
$m(A):=\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|$ denote the maximum-entry norm of a $4\times4$
matrix. Then with
$\varepsilon_*:=\min\{\varepsilon_0,\,L,\,1,\,(128C)^{-1}\}$ the following
hold for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$:

**(a) Smallness, timelikeness and stationarity.** On $K$,

$$m\bigl(E(\varepsilon)\bigr)\le4C\varepsilon,\qquad m\bigl(H(\varepsilon)\bigr)\le16C\varepsilon\le\tfrac18,\qquad g(\varepsilon)_{00}\le-\tfrac12 ,$$

so the chart field $\partial_0$ is timelike on $K$; moreover $\partial_0$ is
a Killing field of $g(\varepsilon)$ on $\Omega$
([[def-gr-killing-field]]).

**(b) Inverse-metric expansion and uniform bounds.** There is
$C_1=C_1(C,L)<\infty$ such that on $K$, with
$R^{ab}(\varepsilon):=g^{ab}(\varepsilon)-\eta^{ab}+\eta^{ac}E_{cd}(\varepsilon)\eta^{db}$,

$$|R^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le C_1\varepsilon^2,\qquad |g^{ab}(\varepsilon)-\eta^{ab}|\le C_1\varepsilon,\qquad |\partial^\alpha g^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le\frac{C_1}{L^{|\alpha|}}\quad(1\le|\alpha|\le2),$$

and

$$|\partial^\alpha R^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le\frac{C_1\varepsilon^2}{L^{|\alpha|}}\qquad(0\le|\alpha|\le2),$$

where $g^{ab}(\varepsilon)$ are the components of the inverse metric
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $M:=\mathbb R^4$ carry its standard smooth structure
([[def-smooth-manifold]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ be the **identity chart**, $x(p)=p$;
it is a global chart of the maximal smooth atlas, and the coordinate
derivations $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3$ form a basis of
$T_pM$ at every $p\in M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). Write

$$\eta:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$$

for the standard Lorentz form of inertia $(3,1,0)$ in this basis
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

**(a) The metric.** Define the covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ on $M$ by the
requirement that its components in the identity chart are the constants

$$g_{ab}:=\eta_{ab}\qquad(a,b=0,1,2,3),$$

that is, $g_p(\partial_a|_p,\partial_b|_p)=\eta_{ab}$ for every $p\in M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]] clause (a)). The component
functions are constant, hence $C^\infty$, so $g$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field; at every $p$ the form $g_p$ is nondegenerate with
inertia $(3,1,0)$. By [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a) the
pair $(M,g)$ is therefore a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$.

**(b) The inertial chart and frame.** The chart $x$ is called the **inertial
chart** of the flat model. In this chart the coordinate frame
$(\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3)$ is a $g$-orthonormal frame at
every point, $g(\partial_a,\partial_b)=\eta_{ab}$; it is simultaneously a
coordinate frame and a **tetrad field** in the sense of
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]], defined on all of $M$.

**(c) Time orientation and causal classification.** Define the smooth vector
field $N:=\partial_0$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). Since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)=\eta_{00}=-1<0$ for every $p$, the field $N$ is everywhere
timelike, so $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). For a nonzero tangent
vector $v=v^a\partial_a|_p$ the definitions of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c) and
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] give

$$g_p(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(v^i)^2,\qquad g_p(v,N_p)=-v^0 .$$

so $v$ is **future-directed** exactly when $v^0>0$, and

- $v$ is future timelike $\iff$ $v^0>0$ and $(v^0)^2>\sum_i(v^i)^2$;
- $v$ is future null $\iff$ $v^0>0$ and $(v^0)^2=\sum_i(v^i)^2$;
- $v$ is spacelike $\iff$ $(v^0)^2<\sum_i(v^i)^2$;

consequently the future causal cone at every point is
$\{v\neq0: v^0\ge\sqrt{\sum_i(v^i)^2}\}$. These are the standard readings of
the Minkowski form in the inertial chart; the chain of equivalences is the
specialization of the causal classification to this pair $(g_p,N_p)$ and is
recorded here for later use.

**(d) Scope.** This item defines geometric data only: a manifold, a metric
field, a time orientation and a distinguished chart and frame. It makes no
claim about curvature, about any field equation, about which geometry a
physical model uses, or about nature; the physical reading of the data, the
dimensions of the coordinates and the numerical values or signs of physical
constants belong to the framework's unit conventions and postulates, which
are separate items. In particular no relation between the coordinate
functions $x^a$ and physical time or length measurements is asserted here.

derivations.claim: (Reparametrization identity.) Write $v^a:=dz^a/ds$ for the affine velocity of the geodesic and $u^a:=dx^a/dt$ for its coordinate-time velocity, so that $v^0=c\,dt/ds\ne0$ and $u^a=c v^a/v^0$; in particular $u^0=c$, so $u=(c,\dot x)$. The geodesic equation of [L2] reads $dv^a/ds=-\Gamma^a{}_{bc}v^bv^c$. Since $v^a=(v^0/c)u^a$, substituting $v^bv^c=(v^0/c)^2u^bu^c$ and using the chain rule $\frac{d}{dt}=\frac{c}{v^0}\frac{d}{ds}$ gives $$\frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2}=\frac{c}{v^0}\frac{d}{ds}\Bigl(\frac{cv^i}{v^0}\Bigr)=\frac{c^2}{(v^0)^2}\frac{dv^i}{ds}-\frac{c^2v^i}{(v^0)^3}\frac{dv^0}{ds}=-\Gamma^i{}_{bc}u^bu^c+\frac{u^i}{c}\Gamma^0{}_{bc}u^bu^c,$$ which is (a).

(Uniform smallness of the velocity data.) The hypothesis $|\dot x|\le C\sqrt\varepsilon c$ and $u^0=c$ give $|u^a|\le\max(c,C\sqrt\varepsilon c)\le C_4c$ for a constant $C_4$ depending only on $C$, since $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*'\le1$ may be assumed after shrinking the threshold.

(Insertion of the bounds.) Insert the components of the identity of step 1.1 and the estimates of [L1], using step 1.2 to bound the velocity factors: $$-c^2\Gamma^i{}_{00}=-\partial_i\Phi+O(c^2\varepsilon^2/L),\qquad |2c\,\Gamma^i{}_{0j}\dot x^j|\le 2c\cdot\frac{C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L}\cdot C\sqrt\varepsilon c=\frac{C'c^2\varepsilon^2}{L},$$ $$|\Gamma^i{}_{jk}\dot x^j\dot x^k|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon}{L}\cdot C^2\varepsilon c^2=\frac{C''c^2\varepsilon^2}{L},$$ and each of the three terms containing the factor $\dot x^i/c$ is bounded by $C'''c^2\varepsilon^2/L$: for the $\Gamma^0{}_{00}$ term, $|\dot x^i| c\,|\Gamma^0{}_{00}|\le C\sqrt\varepsilon c\cdot c\cdot C_2\varepsilon^{5/2}/L=C'''c^2\varepsilon^3/L\le C'''c^2\varepsilon^2/L$; for the $\Gamma^0{}_{0j}$ term, $|2\dot x^i\Gamma^0{}_{0j}\dot x^j|\le2C\sqrt\varepsilon c\cdot C_2\varepsilon/L\cdot C\sqrt\varepsilon c$; and for the $\Gamma^0{}_{jk}$ term, $|\dot x^i\Gamma^0{}_{jk}\dot x^j\dot x^k|/c\le C\sqrt\varepsilon\cdot C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}/L\cdot C^2\varepsilon c^2$. Collecting all terms and renaming the constants gives (b).
(Conclusion.) Step 1.1 proves (a) and step 2.1 proves (b), with constants depending only on $C$, $L$ and the dimension.

boundaries.reason: The geodesic and its parameter interval are nonempty data, and the bounds are pointwise; no empty family arises.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.2 bounds the coordinate velocity components by C₁c, so in particular the zero-velocity case |ẋ| = 0 is inside the hypothesis; step 2.1 inserts the bounds including this case.

boundaries.reason: The spatial dimension is three throughout; no one-dimensional specialization is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: the statement assumes dt/ds ≠ 0 on the parameter interval, which excludes the degenerate case in which the coordinate time fails to parametrize the geodesic; step 1.1 uses exactly this nondegeneracy.

boundaries.reason: The identity and the bound hold at every interior t of the interval I of the coordinate time; no endpoint value is asserted.
The chart, the geodesic and its parametrization are fixed; no selection occurs.
Clause (a) is a reparametrization identity and clause (b) an estimate; no equivalence is asserted.
No converse is claimed; in particular the O(ε²) error bound is not asserted to be sharp.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data
with potential $\Phi=\varepsilon c^2\varphi$
([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]]), let $c>0$, let
$\varepsilon_*$ and $C_2$ be the threshold and constant of
[[lem-gr-weak-field-christoffel-bounds]], let
$0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$, and let $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the
Christoffel symbols of $g(\varepsilon)$ in the inertial chart.

**(a) Reparametrization identity.** Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic of
$g(\varepsilon)$ in an affine parameter $s$ on an interval $S$
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]), suppose that
$t(s):=x^0(\gamma(s))/c$ is $C^2$ with $dt/ds\ne0$ on $S$ and has image an
interval $I$, and write $x(t)$ for the spatial components of
$\gamma$ as a function of $t$, so that $u^a:=dx^a/dt$ is $(c,\dot x)$ and the
geodesic equation holds in the chart
([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]). Then for every $t\in I$,

$$\frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2} =-\Gamma^i{}_{bc}u^bu^c+\frac{u^i}{c}\,\Gamma^0{}_{bc}u^bu^c .$$

**(b) Newtonian leading term.** Suppose in addition that $x(t)\in K$ and
$|\dot x(t)|\le C\sqrt\varepsilon\,c$ for every $t\in I$. Then there is
$C_3<\infty$, depending only on $C$, $L$ and the dimension, such that for
every $t\in I$ and $i=1,2,3$,

$$\Bigl|\frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2}+\partial_i\Phi\bigl(x(t)\bigr)\Bigr|\le\frac{C_3\,c^2\varepsilon^2}{L} .$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim:
(Scaled equation for the geodesic.) Differentiating $X_\varepsilon(S)=x_\varepsilon(t(S))/L$ and $W_\varepsilon(S)=\dot x_\varepsilon(t(S))/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$ with $dt/dS=L/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$ gives $X_\varepsilon'=W_\varepsilon$ and $W_\varepsilon'=\ddot x_\varepsilon L/(\varepsilon c^2)$. By [L1] and $
abla_x\Phi=\varepsilon c^2
abla_x\varphi=\varepsilon c^2L^{-1}
abla_X\psi$, $$W_\varepsilon'=-
abla_X\psi(X_\varepsilon)+R_\varepsilon,\qquad |R_\varepsilon|\le C_3\varepsilon,$$ with $C_3$ depending only on $C$ and $L$: indeed the error is $L/(\varepsilon c^2)$ times the bound $C_2c^2\varepsilon^2/L$ of [L1].
(Newtonian system.) By (H2), $X_*'=W_*$ and $W_*'=-\nabla\psi(X_*)$ on $[0,S_*]$.

(Lipschitz bound for the force.) Since $X_\varepsilon(S),X_*(S)\in K'$ and $K'$ is convex, [L2] applied to $
abla\psi$ on $K'$ gives $|
abla\psi(X_\varepsilon(S))-
abla\psi(X_*(S))|\le K_2|X_\varepsilon(S)-X_*(S)|$ for every $S$: the segment between the two points lies in $K'$ and $|D(
abla\psi)|=|D^2\psi|\le K_2$ there by (H3).

(Integral inequality and Gronwall.) By steps 1.1 and 1.2, for every $S\in[0,S_*]$, $$D(S)\le D(0)+\int_0^S\bigl(|W_\varepsilon-W_*|+|\nabla\psi(X_\varepsilon)-\nabla\psi(X_*)|+|R_\varepsilon|\bigr)\,dS'\le D(0)+C_3\varepsilon S+(1+K_2)\int_0^SD(S')\,dS',$$ where step 1.3 bounds the force term by $K_2|X_\varepsilon-X_*|\le K_2D$ and the velocity term by $D$. The function $a(S):=D(0)+C_3\varepsilon S$ is nondecreasing and $b:=1+K_2$ is constant, so [L3] gives $D(S)\le a(S)e^{(1+K_2)S}\le(D(0)+C_3\varepsilon S_*)e^{(1+K_2)S_*}$.

(Consequences and conclusion.) The displayed estimate is the main claim; (i) and (ii) follow by inserting $D(0)\to0$ respectively $D(0)=0$ and recalling that $C_3$, $K_2$ and $S_*$ are fixed in the limit, while (iii) is the identity $T_\varepsilon=LS_*/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$.

boundaries.evidence: step 3.1 controls the degenerate interval S_* → 0: with matched data D(0) = 0 the bound tends to zero, and at S = 0 the trajectories agree; the intervals [0,T_ε] and [0,S_*] are nonempty for ε > 0 and S_* > 0.

step 3.1 disposes of the special initial-data cases D(0) = 0 and D(0) → 0, which are the zero and limiting cases of the Gronwall bound, and the case S_* = 0 is the trivial empty interval of the estimate.

boundaries.reason: The dimension is three throughout the scaling; no one-dimensional case is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.3 uses convexity of K' and the bound |D²ψ| ≤ K₂ there, so the Lipschitz bound on ∇ψ is available on the whole segment between the trajectories; the case where the segment leaves K' cannot occur by convexity.
step 3.1 evaluates the bound at S = S_* and the integral of step 2.1 runs from 0 to S, covering both endpoints of the scaled interval.

boundaries.reason: The constants C₃ and K₂ are determined by C, L, the dimension and the fixed set K'; the comparison map (X_*,W_*) is a hypothesis.
The theorem is an estimate with convergence corollaries; it does not assert an equivalence.
No converse (for example divergence if the hypotheses fail) is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, let $n$ be an observer at $p$, let $c>0$, and for
$P\in T_pM$ write $E:=E_n(P)$, $q:=q_n(P)$ and $m:=m(P)$ as in
[[def-gr-observer-relative-energy-and-momentum]]. Then:

1. **Master identity.** $E^2=c^2\bigl(g_p(q,q)-g_p(P,P)\bigr)$.
2. **Positivity.** If $P$ is nonzero future causal, then $E>0$.
3. **Mass shell.** If $P$ is future timelike, then $m>0$ and, with
   $U:=P/m$, $u:=U/c$ and $\gamma:=-g_p(n,u)$, one has $\gamma\ge1$,
   $E=mc^2\gamma$, $q=m\gamma w$ where $w:=c\,h_n(u)/\gamma$,
   $g_p(q,q)=m^2c^2(\gamma^2-1)$ and

   $$E^2=m^2c^4+c^2g_p(q,q).$$
4. **Null case.** If $P$ is future null and nonzero, then $E>0$,
   $E=c\sqrt{g_p(q,q)}$ and $E^2=c^2g_p(q,q)$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, let $n$ be an observer at $p$, and let $c>0$ be a real parameter
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observer energy and spatial momentum.** For every $P\in T_pM$ define the
**observer energy** and the **spatial momentum** of $P$ relative to $n$ by

$$E_n(P):=-c\,g_p(P,n),\qquad q_n(P):=h_n(P),$$

where $h_n$ is the spatial projection of the observer $n$. Both maps are
$\mathbb R$-linear in $P$: the first because $g_p$ is bilinear, the second by
[[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]. The second takes values in the
rest space $n^{\perp}$, and by the rest-space decomposition of that lemma every
$P$ has the unique decomposition

$$P=\frac{E_n(P)}{c}\,n+q_n(P),\qquad \frac{E_n(P)}{c}\in\mathbb R,\quad q_n(P)\in n^{\perp}.$$

Equivalently $E_n(P)=c\,\lambda$ and $q_n(P)=w$ for the unique pair
$(\lambda,w)$ with $P=\lambda n+w$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $w\in n^{\perp}$.

**(b) Rest mass and four-velocity normalization.** For $P\in T_pM$ with
$g_p(P,P)\le0$ define the **rest mass**

$$m(P):=\frac{\sqrt{-g_p(P,P)}}{c}\ge0,$$

where the square root is the nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]. By
strict positivity of the square root of a positive number, $m(P)=0$ exactly
when $P=0$ or $P$ is null, and $m(P)>0$ exactly when $P$ is timelike
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). When $m(P)>0$, define the
**normalized four-velocity direction**

$$U(P):=\frac{P}{m(P)},$$

so that $g_p(U(P),U(P))=g_p(P,P)/m(P)^2=-c^2$. Conversely, if $m>0$ and
$U\in T_pM$ satisfy $g_p(U,U)=-c^2$, then $P:=mU$ has $g_p(P,P)=-m^2c^2$ and
$m(P)=m$, $U(P)=U$; the pair $(m,U)$ with $U$ future-directed determines and
is determined by its future timelike $P=mU$.

**(c) Scope and reading.** $E_n$ and $q_n$ depend on the observer $n$: for the
same nonzero $P$, different observers $n,n'$ generally give different values,
and no observer-independent splitting of $P$ into "energy" and "momentum" is
defined by this item. The identities above are algebraic; this definition
asserts no positivity of $E_n$ (that is proved separately), no conservation,
no dynamics and no measurement. The names observer energy, spatial momentum
and rest mass, and their physical units and interpretation, belong to the
physical reading of the framework's unit conventions and postulates and are
not asserted here; this item fixes only the mathematical dependence on the
objects $P$, $n$, $g_p$ and the parameter $c$.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

derivations.claim: (The relative speed and the Lorentz factor.) Combining $q_n=m\gamma w$ with $g_p(q_n,q_n)=m^2c^2(\gamma^2-1)$ from [L1] gives $m^2\gamma^2s^2=m^2c^2(\gamma^2-1)$, hence $\gamma^2(c^2-s^2)=c^2$; since $\gamma\ge1>0$ this reads $\gamma=(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and the identity forces $s<c$ as well as $s^2/c^2=1-\gamma^{-2}$.

(Taylor bounds for the Lorentz factor.) Let $f(z):=(1-z)^{-1/2}$ on $[0,z_0]$ with $z_0<1$. By [L3] and [L2], $$|f(z)-1-\tfrac12z|\le\tfrac12\sup_{t\in[0,z_0]}|f''(t)|z^2=\tfrac38(1-z_0)^{-5/2}z^2,\qquad |f(z)-1|\le\sup_{t\in[0,z_0]}|f'(t)|z=\tfrac12(1-z_0)^{-3/2}z .$$

(Energy and momentum formulas.) By [L1] and step 1.1, $g_p(q_n,q_n)=m^2\gamma^2s^2$ and $\gamma>0$, so $|q_n(P)|=\sqrt{g_p(q_n,q_n)}=m\gamma s$; hence, with $E_n=mc^2\gamma$, $E_n(P)=mc^2(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ and $|q_n(P)|=ms(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$.

(Energy expansion.) Substituting $z=s^2/c^2$ in the first bound of step 1.2 into $E_n=mc^2f(z)$ of step 2.1 gives $|E_n-mc^2-\tfrac12ms^2|\le mc^2\cdot\tfrac38(1-z_0)^{-5/2}(s^4/c^4)=\tfrac38(1-z_0)^{-5/2}ms^4/c^2$.
(Momentum expansion.) Likewise $|q_n|=msf(z)$ by step 2.1, so $||q_n|-ms|=ms|f(z)-1|\le ms\cdot\tfrac12(1-z_0)^{-3/2}(s^2/c^2)=\tfrac12(1-z_0)^{-3/2}ms^3/c^2$.
(Conclusion.) Step 2.1 gives the identities of the statement (including $s<c$), and steps 3.1 and 3.2 give the two uniform error bounds for $s\le v_0<c$.

boundaries.reason: The observer, the momentum and the interval [0,v0] are nonempty data; no empty set is quantified over.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 derives γ²(c²-s²) = c², so the zero-relative-speed case s = 0 gives γ = 1 and the expansions reduce to E = mc² and |q| = 0; the bounds of steps 3.1 and 3.2 then hold trivially with s = 0.

boundaries.reason: No dimension parameter occurs; the lemma is pointwise in one tangent space, and no one-dimensional analogue is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 concludes s < c strictly for any future timelike P, so the degenerate light-cone limit s = c is excluded; the expansion is stated only for s ≤ v0 < c.
step 1.2 takes z ∈ [0,z0] with z0 < 1 and sup on the closed interval, and the bounds are uniform for s ≤ v0, so the endpoint z = z0 is included by the Lagrange remainder hypothesis.

boundaries.reason: The vector P, the observer n and the bound v0 are fixed data; no selection occurs.
The lemma states identities and one-sided Taylor bounds, not an equivalence.
No converse is asserted; the expansion is not claimed to characterize timelike momenta.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ and the chart $x=\psi_p$ on $T_0M$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary with affine connection $\nabla$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ is an **affinely parametrized geodesic** when
$$D_t\gamma'(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$
with one-sided interpretation at an included endpoint. Constant curves are geodesics. Unless another parametrization is explicitly stated, “geodesic” means affinely parametrized geodesic.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $p\in M$,
let $\mathcal E_p\subseteq T_pM$ be the exponential domain and
$\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$ the exponential map of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]], and identify
$T_{h}(T_pM)$ with $T_pM$ by the canonical isomorphism for every
$h\in T_pM$ ([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]).

**(a) The differential in terms of Jacobi fields.** Let $v\in T_pM$, let
$s_1>0$ satisfy $s_1v\in\mathcal E_p$, and let $u\in T_pM$. Let
$\gamma:[0,s_1]\to M$, $\gamma(t):=\exp_p(tv)$ (well defined by star-shapedness
of $\mathcal E_p$), and let $J_u$ be the unique Jacobi field along
$\gamma$ with $J_u(0)=0$ and $D_tJ_u(0)=u$
([[thm-gr-jacobi-equation-and-geodesic-deviation]] clause (c),
[[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]] clause (b)). Then
$$d(\exp_p)_{tv}(tu)=J_u(t)\qquad(0\le t\le s_1);$$
in particular $d(\exp_p)_{s_1v}(s_1u)=J_u(s_1)$ and, in the special case
$s_1=1$, $v\in\mathcal E_p$, $d(\exp_p)_v(u)=J_u(1)$.

**(b) Conjugacy as a kernel condition.** With the notation of (a),
$d(\exp_p)_{s_1v}$ is injective if and only if no nonzero Jacobi field
along $\gamma$ vanishes at $t=0$ and at $t=s_1$. Moreover
$\ker d(\exp_p)_{s_1v}=s_1\{u\in T_pM:J_u(s_1)=0\}$, so
$\dim\ker d(\exp_p)_{s_1v}$ equals the multiplicity of the conjugate
instant $s_1$ whenever $\gamma(s_1)$ is conjugate to $p$ along $\gamma$
([[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]] clause (d)).

**(c) Conjugate instants of a geodesic.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a smooth
geodesic with $\gamma(0)=p$, and let $s_1>0$ with $s_1\in I$ and
$s_1\gamma'(0)\in\mathcal E_p$. Then $\gamma(s_1)$ is conjugate to
$\gamma(0)=p$ along $\gamma$ if and only if $d(\exp_p)_{s_1\gamma'(0)}$ is
not injective.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $R$ be its
curvature ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]), let
$I,J_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be intervals with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]), and let $F:J_0\times I\to M$ be a smooth map. Write
$T:=\partial_tF$ and $J^F:=\partial_rF$; a field along $F$ means a smooth
section of $F^*TM$ over $J_0\times I$, and $D_r,D_t$ are the covariant
derivatives in the two parameters
([[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Curvature as the commutator of the two derivatives.** For every smooth
field $V$ along $F$,
$$\bigl(D_tD_r-D_rD_t\bigr)V=R(T,J^F)V .$$

**(b) Geodesic deviation.** Suppose in addition that for every $r\in J_0$ the
curve $t\mapsto F(r,t)$ is a geodesic with affine parameter $t$, that is
$D_tT=0$. Then $D_tJ^F=D_rT$ and
$$D_t^2J^F=R(T,J^F)T .$$
Consequently, for every $r$ the field $t\mapsto J^F(r,t)$ is a Jacobi field
along the geodesic $t\mapsto F(r,t)$
([[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]] clause (b)), and for a geodesic
variation the variation field is a Jacobi field.

**(c) Initial data.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a smooth geodesic and let
$s_0\in I$. For every pair $J_0,J_1\in T_{\gamma(s_0)}M$ there exists exactly
one smooth Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ with
$$J(s_0)=J_0,\qquad D_sJ(s_0)=J_1 .$$
The set of all Jacobi fields along $\gamma$ is a real vector space of
dimension $8$, and $J\mapsto\bigl(J(s_0),D_sJ(s_0)\bigr)$ is a linear
isomorphism onto $T_{\gamma(s_0)}M\oplus T_{\gamma(s_0)}M$.

**(d) The tangential component.** Let $\gamma$ be a smooth geodesic and $J$ a
smooth Jacobi field along it. Then $s\mapsto g(J,\gamma')(s)$ is affine, and
if $\gamma$ is future timelike with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-1$, the normal
component $J^\perp=J-g(J,\gamma')\gamma'$ is again a Jacobi field along
$\gamma$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
$R$ be its curvature ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Let
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an affinely parametrized
geodesic with $D_s\gamma'=0$, written $T:=\gamma'$
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]); the parameter is the affinely
parametrized one of that definition and need not be proper time.

**(a) Fields along $\gamma$ and the derivative $D_s$.** A **field along
$\gamma$** is a section $J$ of the pullback bundle $\gamma^*TM$, and $D_s$
denotes the covariant derivative along $\gamma$ of
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. A field is **smooth** when its
coefficients in a smooth local frame of $M$ around each point of $\gamma$ are
$C^\infty$ on the corresponding parameter interval. At an included endpoint
of $I$ all derivatives below are one-sided.

**(b) Jacobi field.** A **Jacobi field along $\gamma$** is a smooth field $J$
along $\gamma$ satisfying the **Jacobi equation**
$$D_s^2J=R(T,J)T\qquad(s\in I),$$
that is $D_s^2J=R(\gamma',J)\gamma'$. The assignment
$J\mapsto R(T,J)T$, which associates with a field along $\gamma$ another
field along $\gamma$ and is $\mathbb R$-linear, is the **Jacobi operator of
$\gamma$**. Whether the field is smooth only piecewise is stated whenever a
statement uses piecewise fields; the unqualified term means globally smooth.

**(c) Geodesic variations.** A **geodesic variation with affine
parameter $s$** is a smooth map $F:J_0\times I\to M$, where
$J_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with nonempty interior, such that
for every $r\in J_0$ the curve $s\mapsto F(r,s)$ is a geodesic with affine
parameter $s$. Its **variation field** is the field $s\mapsto\partial_rF(r,s)$
along the curve $s\mapsto F(0,s)$. The variation field of a geodesic
variation is a Jacobi field along that curve
([[thm-gr-jacobi-equation-and-geodesic-deviation]] clause (c)).

**(d) Conjugate instants and multiplicity.** Let $s_0<s_1$ be points of $I$.
The event $\gamma(s_1)$ is **conjugate to** $\gamma(s_0)$ **along $\gamma$**
when there is a nonzero Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ with
$J(s_0)=J(s_1)=0$. In that case $s_1$ is called a **conjugate instant** of
$\gamma$ (with respect to $s_0$, when the base point needs to be named), and
the **multiplicity** of the conjugate instant is the dimension of the real
vector space of Jacobi fields vanishing at $s_0$ and $s_1$; the fields
vanishing at $s_0$ form a $4$-dimensional space and the multiplicity is at
most $4$, since a Jacobi field is determined by its value and derivative at
$s_0$ ([[thm-gr-jacobi-equation-and-geodesic-deviation]] clause (d)). For a
geodesic with $\gamma(s_0)=p$ and $\gamma'(s_0)=v$, the corresponding
possibility of conjugacy is measured by the derivative of the exponential
map at $s_1v$
([[lem-gr-conjugacy-via-the-exponential-map]]); that equivalence is proved,
not assumed here. No conjugate instant is asserted to exist.

**(e) The normal bundle.** If $\gamma$ is future timelike with
$g(T,T)=-1$, define the **normal bundle** $N_\gamma$ to be the family of
smooth fields $J$ along $\gamma$ with $g(J,T)=0$, and write $|J|:=\sqrt{g(J,J)}$
for $J\in N_\gamma$. Then $N_\gamma$ is a rank-three subbundle of
$\gamma^*TM$, $g$ restricts to a positive definite inner product on each
fibre, and $D_s$ preserves $N_\gamma$, because
$\frac{d}{ds}g(J,T)=g(D_sJ,T)+g(J,D_sT)=g(D_sJ,T)$ with $D_sT=0$; these
statements are proved in [[lem-gr-normal-index-form-factorization]] clause
(b). The **normal component** of a field $V$ is
$V^\perp:=V-g(V,T)T$ when $g(T,T)=-1$.

For a given connection on $E$ and a smooth curve on an interval with nonempty interior, the **covariant derivative along the curve** is
$$D_tV=(\gamma^*\nabla)_{\partial/\partial t}V.$$
Here $V$ is a section of the pullback bundle as in [[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]], and the pullback connection exists by [[thm-pullback-connection-is-well-defined-and-functorial]]. It is real-linear and satisfies $D_t(fV)=f'V+fD_tV$ for functions of the parameter.

At an included endpoint the smooth up-to-boundary coefficients have their one-sided derivative; equivalently any smooth local extension of the coefficients gives this value, because extensions agreeing on a one-sided interval have the same derivative there. For a piecewise smooth curve the derivative is defined on each piece, with separate one-sided derivatives at corners; those derivatives are not required to agree. A singleton interval carries no derivative operator under this convention and will have identity transport by definition. A zero section or a rank-zero bundle gives zero covariant derivative. Constant base curves can have sections with nonzero coefficient derivative.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection; its existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. For a
smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ write $D_t$ for the covariant derivative along
$\gamma$ of [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]] with respect to
$\nabla$ (equivalently, the pullback of the Levi–Civita connection).

1. **Metric pairing.** For smooth sections $V,W$ of the pullback bundle
   $\gamma^*TM$,
   $$\frac{d}{dt}\,g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),W(t)\bigr)=g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(D_tV(t),W(t)\bigr)+g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),D_tW(t)\bigr).$$
   In particular, if $D_tV=D_tW=0$ on $I$, then $g(V,W)$ is constant on $I$.

2. **Parallel transport.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise smooth curve.
   For every $v\in T_{\gamma(a)}M$ there is exactly one continuous piecewise
   smooth section $V$ of $\gamma^*TM$ with $D_tV=0$ on each smooth piece and
   $V(a)=v$; the parallel-transport map
   $P_\gamma:T_{\gamma(a)}M\to T_{\gamma(b)}M$, $v\mapsto V(b)$, is linear,
   bijective, and satisfies
   $g_{\gamma(b)}(P_\gamma v,P_\gamma w)=g_{\gamma(a)}(v,w)$ for all $v,w$.

3. **Geodesic speed and affine parameter.** Along a geodesic
   $\gamma:I\to M$ ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]) the norm
   $g(\gamma',\gamma')$ is constant, so the causal character of $\gamma$
   (timelike, null or spacelike) is constant on $I$; a nonzero constant value
   makes $\gamma$ regular on all of $I$. If $\gamma$ is timelike and
   $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-\lambda^2$ with $\lambda>0$, then the proper-time
   increment of $\gamma$ over $[t_0,t]$ is $\lambda(t-t_0)/c$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]), so proper time is an
   affine parameter of $\gamma$; the four-velocity
   $U=\lambda^{-1}\gamma'$ is parallel, $D_\tau U=0$ in the proper-time
   parameter. A null geodesic has $g(\gamma',\gamma')=0$ and admits no
   proper-time parametrization.

4. **Affine reparametrizations.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a geodesic and let
   $h:J\to I$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its open image with $h'\neq0$.
   Then $\gamma\circ h$ is a geodesic if and only if $h(s)=as+b$ with
   constants $a\neq0$, $b$; in that case $a$ is the constant
   $h'$, and every affine parameter of $\gamma$ arises in this way from a
   fixed one.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth and let $p\in M$. The **differential of $F$ at $p$** is the map $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ defined by
$$ dF_p(v)([g]):=v([g\circ F]) $$
for every derivation $v\in T_pM$ and every germ $[g]\in C_{F(p)}^\infty(N)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
