boundaries.evidence: step 3.1 records s = c/2 < c, so the light-cone degenerate case is excluded; the bound's constant is evaluated at z0 = 1/4 < 1.

boundaries.reason: The checks are at a single interior relative speed; no interval endpoint is evaluated.
The vectors, the observer and the speed ratio are explicitly fixed.
The example checks identities and inequalities; no equivalence is asserted.
The check verifies the lemma's identities and bounds at one relative speed; it asserts no converse direction such as sharpness of the bounds.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g_\eta,N_\eta)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set identified with its chart image,
and let $c>0$ and $G_N>0$ be real parameters; put
$\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$ as in the framework's convention. All components below
are taken in the inertial chart, and $\partial_a$ are the chart derivatives.

**(a) Structural data.** A tuple $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ is
**stationary weak-field data** when

- $K\subseteq\Omega$ is a compact set, $L>0$, $C>0$ and
  $\varepsilon_0>0$ are constants;
- $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth dimensionless function and
  $r=(r_{ab})$ is a family of component functions
  $r_{ab}(\varepsilon,p)$, defined for $\varepsilon\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
  and $p\in\Omega$ for some $\varepsilon_1>\varepsilon_0$ and smooth in
  $(\varepsilon,p)$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]);
- for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\varepsilon,p)=\begin{cases}-(1+2\varepsilon\varphi(p))+r_{00}(\varepsilon,p),&a=b=0,\\[2pt] r_{0i}(\varepsilon,p),&\{a,b\}=\{0,i\},\\[2pt] (1-2\varepsilon\varphi(p))\,\delta_{ij}+r_{ij}(\varepsilon,p),&a=i,\ b=j,\end{cases}$$

  is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\varepsilon)$ on
  $\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]);
- **(stationarity)** $\partial_0\varphi=0$ and $\partial_0r_{ab}=0$ on
  $\Omega$ for all $a,b$ and all $\varepsilon$, so that
  $\partial_0g_{ab}(\varepsilon,\cdot)=0$;
- **(bounds)** for every multiindex $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le2$ and every
  $p\in K$,

$$|\partial^\alpha\varphi(p)|\le\frac{C}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{00}(\varepsilon,p)|+|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}(\varepsilon,p)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^2}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{0i}(\varepsilon,p)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L^{|\alpha|}} .$$

  (Here $|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}|$ stands for the maximum over $i,j$ and
  $|\partial^\alpha r_{0i}|$ for the maximum over $i$.)

**(b) Derived data.** For stationary weak-field data define the
**potential**

$$\Phi:=\varepsilon c^2\varphi\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$

a smooth stationary function of dimension $\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-2}$ in
the framework's unit conventions. The symmetric component family
$g(\varepsilon)-\eta$ is the **perturbation of the family**.

**(c) Einstein families.** Stationary weak-field data form an **Einstein
family with coupling $\kappa$** when for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$
there is a smooth symmetric component field $T_{ab}(\varepsilon,\cdot)$ on
$\Omega$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) satisfying

$$G_{ab}\bigl(g(\varepsilon)\bigr)=\kappa\,T_{ab}(\varepsilon)\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$

where $G$ is the Einstein tensor of the metric-selected connection of
$g(\varepsilon)$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). In that case define the
**density read from the time-time component**

$$\rho_\varepsilon:=\frac{T_{00}(\varepsilon)}{c^2}\qquad\text{on }\Omega .$$

**(d) Scope.** This item fixes a class of metric families and the vocabulary
of the weak-field bridge: the component form, the stationarity of the data,
the derivative bounds, the potential, and the equation that upgrades the
data to an Einstein family. It asserts that no family exists, that
$\partial_0$ is a Killing field or timelike, that the inverse metrics are
uniformly bounded or that the density is positive; those are consequences
proved separately where they are used. The family is an explicit
input-family hypothesis: neither its existence for prescribed Newtonian
initial data nor its construction from other data is claimed. The physical
reading of the components, of $G_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$, of $\Phi$ and of
$\rho_\varepsilon$ belongs to the framework's postulates and unit
conventions, which are separate items.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data
that form an Einstein family with coupling $\kappa>0$
([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]] clauses (a)-(c)), with potential
$\Phi=\varepsilon c^2\varphi$ and densities $\rho_\varepsilon$, and let
$G^{(1)}$ be the first-order Einstein coefficient of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]]. Let $c>0$ and $G_N:=\kappa c^4/(8\pi)$.
Then there are
$\varepsilon_*'>0$ and $C_2<\infty$, depending only on $C$, $L$ and the
dimension, such that for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*'$ the following
undirected component inequalities hold on $K$, with the maximum over
$a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and the Laplacian $\Delta$ of the spatial coordinates
([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]):

**(a) Linearized approximation.** With $A_{ab}(\varepsilon):=g_{ab}(\varepsilon)-\eta_{ab}$,

$$\bigl|G_{ab}(g(\varepsilon))-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A(\varepsilon))\bigr|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^2}{L^2} .$$

**(b) Component hierarchy of the Einstein tensor.**

$$\Bigl|G_{00}(g(\varepsilon))-\frac{2\Delta\Phi}{c^2}\Bigr|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^2}{L^2},\qquad |G_{ij}(g(\varepsilon))|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^2}{L^2},\qquad |G_{0i}(g(\varepsilon))|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L^2}.$$

**(c) Stress-energy hierarchy and the Poisson equation.** Since
$G_{ab}(g(\varepsilon))=\kappa T_{ab}(\varepsilon)$,

$$\Bigl|\kappa T_{00}(\varepsilon)-\frac{2\Delta\Phi}{c^2}\Bigr|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^2}{L^2},\qquad |\kappa T_{ij}(\varepsilon)|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^2}{L^2},\qquad |\kappa T_{0i}(\varepsilon)|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L^2}.$$

If in addition the matter hierarchy
$|T_{00}(\varepsilon)-\rho_\varepsilon c^2|\le C\varepsilon^2c^4/(G_NL^2)$
holds on $K$, then

$$|\Delta\Phi-4\pi G_N\rho_\varepsilon|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^2c^2}{L^2}\qquad\text{on }K .$$

**(d) Scaled form.** Let $X:=x/L$ denote the scaled spatial coordinates and
define on the scaled region the functions $\psi(X):=\varphi(LX)$ and
$R(X):=G_NL^2\rho_\varepsilon(LX)/(\varepsilon c^2)$, with $\Delta_X$ the
Laplacian in the $X$-variables. Then

$$|\Delta_X\psi-4\pi R|\le C_2\varepsilon\qquad\text{on the scaled image of }K .$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be an open set of the flat model
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], let
$(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over $\Omega$ with
first-order coefficients $\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}$, $S^{(1)}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}$ and with trace
reversal $\bar h$, d'Alembertian $\Box$ and gauge transformation
$h'_{ab}=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ as in
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]], and let $L>0$ be a length scale.
All components are taken in the inertial chart and all contractions are
with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$.

**(a) Christoffel symbols.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there is a
constant $C_K<\infty$ such that for all $p\in K$ and
$0<|\lambda|\le\varepsilon_1/2$,

$$\Bigl|\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,\eta^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bh_{cd}+\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(b) Ricci tensor.** With the same constants (enlarged if necessary),

$$\Bigl|\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_c\partial_a h^{c}{}_{b}+\partial_c\partial_b h^{c}{}_{a}-\Box h_{ab}-\partial_a\partial_b h\bigr).$$

**(c) Scalar curvature and Einstein tensor.** With the same constants,

$$\Bigl|S(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,S^{(1)}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad S^{(1)}=\partial_a\partial_bh^{ab}-\Box h,$$

and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,G^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h_{ab}+\partial^c\partial_{(a}\bar h_{b)c}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}.$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on
$\Omega$,

$$\bar h'{}_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a+\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\xi_c,\qquad \partial^a\bar h'{}_{ab}=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}-\Box\xi_b .$$

Consequently $h'$ is in harmonic gauge exactly when
$\Box\xi_b=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}$, and in that case

$$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h'{}_{ab}.$$

**(e) Gauge invariance of the first-order curvature.** For every smooth
covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,

$$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h),\qquad S^{(1)}(h')=S^{(1)}(h),\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=G^{(1)}_{ab}(h).$$

That is, subtracting the pure-gauge perturbation
$\partial_a\xi_b+\partial_b\xi_a$ from the first-order perturbation leaves
the first-order Ricci, scalar and Einstein tensors unchanged; their
first-order coefficients depend on $h$ only through its gauge-equivalence
class.

**(f) Quadratic remainder.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there are
$\delta_0>0$ and $C_K<\infty$ such that for every smooth symmetric component
field $A=(A_{ab})$ on a neighborhood of $K$ with

$$B_K(A):=\sup_K\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|+L^{-1}\sup_K\max_{a,b,c}|\partial_cA_{ab}|+L^{-2}\sup_K\max_{a,b,c,d}|\partial_c\partial_dA_{ab}|\le\delta_0,$$

the metric $\eta+A$ is Lorentzian of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $K$ and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+A)(p)-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)(p)\Bigr|\le \frac{C_K\,B_K(A)^2}{L^2}\qquad(p\in K),$$

where $G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)$ is the right-hand side of the displayed formula of
(c) with $h$ replaced by $A$, and $G_{ab}(\eta+A)$ is the Einstein tensor of
the metric with components $\eta_{ab}+A_{ab}$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h$ on $\Omega$ with components $h_{ab}$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) — the **first-order
perturbation** — and a smooth family $q$ of symmetric component fields
$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
and $p\in\Omega$, such that for every $\lambda$ with
$0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\lambda)$ on
$\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $q$ is the **normalized remainder**. The
family is thus normalized so that $g(0)=\eta$ is its value at
$\lambda=0$ and $h=\partial_\lambda g(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}$. No assumption
is made that $g(\lambda)$ solves any field equation; the metrics $g(\lambda)$
are the mathematical input of the linearization.

**(b) First-order coefficients.** Let $A(\lambda)$ stand for any of the
component families $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))$, $S(g(\lambda))$,
$G_{ab}(g(\lambda))$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\lambda)$; these
are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ because the Christoffel symbols, the curvature
components and the inverse metric are smooth functions of the metric
components and their derivatives
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Define the **first-order
coefficients**

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and
lowered with the flat metric $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{ab}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]): $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$,
$h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$, and

$$\Box:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b=-\partial_0^2+\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2$$

is the **d'Alembertian** of the flat metric, applied componentwise to
component families. The **trace** of $h$ and the **trace-reversed
perturbation** are

$$h:=\eta^{ab}h_{ab},\qquad \bar h_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,h\,\eta_{ab} .$$

The inverse passage is the same formula, $\bar h_{ab}$'s trace being
$\eta^{ab}\bar h_{ab}=h-2h=-h$: explicitly

$$h_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\eta^{cd}\bar h_{cd} .$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For a smooth covector field $\xi_b$ on
$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: (The data clauses.) The component fields $g_{ab}(\varepsilon,p)=\eta_{ab}+\varepsilon h_{ab}(p)$ are polynomial in $(\varepsilon,p)$, hence smooth; they are stationary; and for $0<|\varepsilon|\le1/2$ and $p\in\Omega$ one has $|2\varepsilon\varphi(p)|<2\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac12<1$ because $\varphi<1/2$ on $\Omega$, so by [L5] they define a smooth Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $\Omega$. The bounds on $K$ hold with $C=L=1$: $|\varphi|=\frac12|\mathbf x|^2\le\frac12\cdot\frac14=\frac18\le1$; $|\partial_i\varphi|=|x^i|\le\frac12\le1$; $|\partial_i\partial_j\varphi|=\delta_{ij}\le1$; and $r\equiv0$ satisfies the $r$-bounds trivially. With $\varepsilon_1:=\varepsilon_0=1/2$ the family $(\varepsilon_1,h,q\equiv0)$ satisfies [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (a) and $g(\varepsilon)-\eta=\varepsilon h$. This proves clause 1.

(First-order coefficient.) By [L3], $\Delta\varphi=3$ and $h$ is stationary, so $\Box\bar h_{00}=\Delta(-4\varphi)=-12$ and $\Box\bar h_{0i}=\Box\bar h_{ij}=0$. By [L4] the closed formula gives $G^{(1)}_{00}=-\frac12(-12)=6$ for $h$; the divergence terms vanish because $\bar h_{ab}=-4\varphi\,\delta_{a0}\delta_{b0}$ has no space-time or spatial components and is stationary, and $\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}=\eta^{00}\eta^{00}\partial_0\partial_0\bar h_{00}=0$. By the same formula every component $G^{(1)}_{0i}$ and $G^{(1)}_{ij}$ is a combination of components $\bar h_{0\cdot}$ or of time derivatives, hence $0$. Since $A(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon h$ and the formula of [L4] is linear in $h$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}(A(\varepsilon))=\varepsilon G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)$; thus $G^{(1)}_{00}(A(\varepsilon))=6\varepsilon$ and $G^{(1)}_{0i}(A(\varepsilon))=G^{(1)}_{ij}(A(\varepsilon))=0$.

(Einstein family and the matter hierarchy.) Define $T_{ab}(\varepsilon):=G_{ab}(g(\varepsilon))/\kappa$ on $\Omega$; the metric-selected connection and its curvature are smooth in the metric components, so $T(\varepsilon)$ is a smooth symmetric component field and $G_{ab}(g(\varepsilon))=\kappa T_{ab}(\varepsilon)$ holds identically; hence the data are an Einstein family and clause (c) of [L1] defines $\rho_\varepsilon=T_{00}/c^2$. With this $\rho_\varepsilon$ the matter hierarchy of [L2] holds with left-hand side $0$, so the theorem applies and provides $\varepsilon_*'$ and $C_2$ depending only on $C=L=1$ and the dimension.

(Poisson equation and density.) Let $\Phi:=\varepsilon c^2\varphi$; by [L3], $\Delta\Phi=\varepsilon c^2\Delta\varphi=3\varepsilon c^2$ on $\Omega$. With $\bar\rho:=3\varepsilon c^2/(4\pi G_N)$ this gives $\Delta\Phi=4\pi G_N\bar\rho$ exactly. Moreover clause (c) of [L2] gives $|\kappa T_{00}-2\Delta\Phi/c^2|\le C_2\varepsilon^2$ on $K$ for $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*'$, that is $|\kappa c^2\rho_\varepsilon-6\varepsilon c^2|\le C_2\varepsilon^2$, which after division by $\kappa c^2>0$ reads $|\rho_\varepsilon-3\varepsilon c^2/(4\pi G_N)|\le C_2\varepsilon^2/(\kappa c^2)=C_2\varepsilon^2c^2/(8\pi G_N)$ by $1/(\kappa c^2)=c^2/(8\pi G_N)$.

(The leading term.) By steps 1.2 and 3.1, $2\Delta\Phi/c^2=2\cdot3\varepsilon c^2/c^2=6\varepsilon=G^{(1)}_{00}(A(\varepsilon))$, so the leading term in the hierarchy inequality $|G_{00}-2\Delta\Phi/c^2|\le C_2\varepsilon^2$ of [L2] is exactly the first-order coefficient of the family, and the residual is the quadratic remainder of [[thm-gr-flat-linearized-curvature-and-gauge]] clause (f); also $G^{(1)}_{0i}=G^{(1)}_{ij}=0$ by step 1.2. This completes the verification of clauses 3 and 4.

boundaries.reason: Ω is the nonempty unit ball and K the nonempty closed ball of radius 1/2; no empty set arises.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 verifies the bounds at the origin and step 3.1 evaluates ΔΦ = 3εc²; the potential vanishes at x = 0, which is the interior minimum included in the bounds |φ| ≤ 1/8.

boundaries.reason: The dimension is four; no one-dimensional specialization is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 checks |2εφ| < 1/2 on Ω for 0 < |ε| ≤ 1/2, so the metric stays Lorentzian and the degenerate smallness boundary is excluded explicitly.

boundaries.reason: All bounds are on the fixed compact K and for 0 < ε ≤ ε_*'; no interval endpoint value is asserted.
The constants L, C, ε0 and the density are fixed explicitly; no selection occurs.
The example exhibits data and computes dictionary quantities; no equivalence is asserted.
No converse (for example uniqueness of the density) is claimed.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g_\eta,N_\eta)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set identified with its chart image,
and let $c>0$ and $G_N>0$ be real parameters; put
$\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$ as in the framework's convention. All components below
are taken in the inertial chart, and $\partial_a$ are the chart derivatives.

**(a) Structural data.** A tuple $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ is
**stationary weak-field data** when

- $K\subseteq\Omega$ is a compact set, $L>0$, $C>0$ and
  $\varepsilon_0>0$ are constants;
- $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth dimensionless function and
  $r=(r_{ab})$ is a family of component functions
  $r_{ab}(\varepsilon,p)$, defined for $\varepsilon\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
  and $p\in\Omega$ for some $\varepsilon_1>\varepsilon_0$ and smooth in
  $(\varepsilon,p)$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]);
- for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\varepsilon,p)=\begin{cases}-(1+2\varepsilon\varphi(p))+r_{00}(\varepsilon,p),&a=b=0,\\[2pt] r_{0i}(\varepsilon,p),&\{a,b\}=\{0,i\},\\[2pt] (1-2\varepsilon\varphi(p))\,\delta_{ij}+r_{ij}(\varepsilon,p),&a=i,\ b=j,\end{cases}$$

  is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\varepsilon)$ on
  $\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]);
- **(stationarity)** $\partial_0\varphi=0$ and $\partial_0r_{ab}=0$ on
  $\Omega$ for all $a,b$ and all $\varepsilon$, so that
  $\partial_0g_{ab}(\varepsilon,\cdot)=0$;
- **(bounds)** for every multiindex $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le2$ and every
  $p\in K$,

$$|\partial^\alpha\varphi(p)|\le\frac{C}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{00}(\varepsilon,p)|+|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}(\varepsilon,p)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^2}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{0i}(\varepsilon,p)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L^{|\alpha|}} .$$

  (Here $|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}|$ stands for the maximum over $i,j$ and
  $|\partial^\alpha r_{0i}|$ for the maximum over $i$.)

**(b) Derived data.** For stationary weak-field data define the
**potential**

$$\Phi:=\varepsilon c^2\varphi\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$

a smooth stationary function of dimension $\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-2}$ in
the framework's unit conventions. The symmetric component family
$g(\varepsilon)-\eta$ is the **perturbation of the family**.

**(c) Einstein families.** Stationary weak-field data form an **Einstein
family with coupling $\kappa$** when for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$
there is a smooth symmetric component field $T_{ab}(\varepsilon,\cdot)$ on
$\Omega$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) satisfying

$$G_{ab}\bigl(g(\varepsilon)\bigr)=\kappa\,T_{ab}(\varepsilon)\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$

where $G$ is the Einstein tensor of the metric-selected connection of
$g(\varepsilon)$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). In that case define the
**density read from the time-time component**

$$\rho_\varepsilon:=\frac{T_{00}(\varepsilon)}{c^2}\qquad\text{on }\Omega .$$

**(d) Scope.** This item fixes a class of metric families and the vocabulary
of the weak-field bridge: the component form, the stationarity of the data,
the derivative bounds, the potential, and the equation that upgrades the
data to an Einstein family. It asserts that no family exists, that
$\partial_0$ is a Killing field or timelike, that the inverse metrics are
uniformly bounded or that the density is positive; those are consequences
proved separately where they are used. The family is an explicit
input-family hypothesis: neither its existence for prescribed Newtonian
initial data nor its construction from other data is claimed. The physical
reading of the components, of $G_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$, of $\Phi$ and of
$\rho_\varepsilon$ belongs to the framework's postulates and unit
conventions, which are separate items.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.
For $n\ge1$, $c\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and $r>0$, the Euclidean closed ball $\overline B_2(c,r)$ and Euclidean sphere $S_2(c,r)$ are compact.

Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data
with potential $\Phi=\varepsilon c^2\varphi$ and $c>0$
([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]]), let $\varepsilon_*$ and $C_2$ be
the threshold and constant of
[[lem-gr-weak-field-christoffel-bounds]], let $S_*>0$ and
$0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$, and put $T_\varepsilon:=LS_*/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$
and $\psi(X):=\varphi(LX)$ on the scaled region.

Suppose:

- **(H1)** for every $t\in[0,T_\varepsilon]$ a geodesic $\gamma_\varepsilon$
  of $g(\varepsilon)$ has spatial trajectory $x_\varepsilon(t)\in K$ in the
  coordinate-time parametrization $x^0(\gamma_\varepsilon(t))=ct$ with
  $|\dot x_\varepsilon(t)|\le C\sqrt\varepsilon c$;
- **(H2)** setting $t(S):=LS/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$,
  $X_\varepsilon(S):=x_\varepsilon(t(S))/L$ and
  $W_\varepsilon(S):=\dot x_\varepsilon(t(S))/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$ for
  $S\in[0,S_*]$, and letting $K'\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a compact convex set
  containing every $X_\varepsilon(S)$, there is a $C^1$ map
  $(X_*,W_*):[0,S_*]\to\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3$ with
  $X_*([0,S_*])\subseteq K'$ and

$$X_*'(S)=W_*(S),\qquad W_*'(S)=-\nabla\psi\bigl(X_*(S)\bigr)\qquad(0\le S\le S_*);$$

- **(H3)** $|D^2\psi|\le K_2$ on $K'$ for a constant $K_2$.

Then for every $S\in[0,S_*]$, with
$D(S):=\bigl|X_\varepsilon(S)-X_*(S)\bigr|+\bigl|W_\varepsilon(S)-W_*(S)\bigr|$
and the Euclidean norm,

$$D(S)\le\bigl(D(0)+C_3\varepsilon S_*\bigr)\,e^{(1+K_2)S_*},$$

where $C_3$ depends only on $C$, $L$ and the dimension. Consequently the
following hold.

**(i) Convergence.** If $D(0)\to0$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ along the
family, then $\sup_{0\le S\le S_*}D(S)\to0$.

**(ii) Rate for identical data.** If $D(0)=0$, then
$\sup_{0\le S\le S_*}D(S)\le C_3\varepsilon S_*e^{(1+K_2)S_*}=O(\varepsilon)$.

**(iii) Long coordinate times.** The coordinate-time horizon is
$T_\varepsilon=LS_*/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$, so the fixed scaled interval
$[0,S_*]$ corresponds to coordinate times growing like
$\varepsilon^{-1/2}$; the limit statement is therefore not a large-$t$
statement at fixed $\varepsilon$.

derivations.claim: (Data and scaled potential.) All components are polynomial and stationary; and for $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0=1/2$ one has $|2\varepsilon\varphi|<1$ on $\Omega$, so the metric has signature $(-,+,+,+)$ by diagonal sign; the bounds $|\varphi|\le1/8\le C$, $|\partial_i\varphi|\le1/2\le C/L$, $|\partial_i\partial_j\varphi|=\delta_{ij}\le1\le C/L^2$ hold on $K$ because $C=1+L^2\ge1\ge L/2$ and $C\ge L^2$; $r\equiv0$ satisfies the $r$-bounds. Hence the tuple is stationary weak-field data. By [L2], $\psi(X)=\varphi(LX)=\frac12|LX|^2=\frac12L^2|X|^2$, $\partial_i\psi(X)=L(LX)^i=L^2X^i$ and $\partial_i\partial_j\psi=L^2\delta_{ij}$, so $\nabla\psi(X)=L^2X$ and $|D^2\psi|\le L^2$ on all of $\mathbb R^3$.

(The explicit solution.) Define $X_*,W_*$ by the displayed formulas. By [L3] and linearity of the derivative, $X_*'(S)=-L\sin(LS)X_0+\cos(LS)W_0=W_*(S)$ and $W_*'(S)=-L^2\cos(LS)X_0-L\sin(LS)W_0=-L^2X_*(S)=-\nabla\psi(X_*(S))$ by step 1.1. So $(X_*,W_*)$ solves the comparison system on $[0,S_*]$ (indeed on $\mathbb R$), and it is $C^1$.

(Compact convex range and hypotheses.) By [L3] and step 2.1, $|X_*(S)|\le|\cos(LS)|\,|X_0|+\frac{|\sin(LS)|}{L}|W_0|\le|X_0|+|W_0|/L=R$ for every $S$, so the range of $X_*$ on $[0,S_*]$ is contained in $\overline B_2(0,R)$; by [L4] that closed ball is compact and convex. Therefore (H2) and (H3) of [L5] hold for these data with $K'=\overline B_2(0,R)$ and $K_2=L^2$, and $X_*,W_*$ are $C^1$ on $[0,S_*]$ with range in $K'$.

(Conclusion.) If in addition a family of geodesics satisfies (H1) of [L5] on $[0,T_\varepsilon]$ with scaled initial data matching $(X_0,W_0)$ at $S=0$, so that $D(0)=0$, then [L5] gives $\sup_{0\le S\le S_*}D(S)\le C_3\varepsilon S_*e^{(1+L^2)S_*}=O(\varepsilon)$: the scaled gravitational trajectory tracks the harmonic oscillator $X_*$ with amplitude $R$ and period $2\pi/L$ to order $\varepsilon$ on the fixed scaled interval, corresponding to coordinate times $T_\varepsilon=LS_*/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$ by clause (iii) of [L5]. This exhibits a case in which every hypothesis of the theorem except (H1) is verified explicitly; (H1) remains a hypothesis on the geodesic family.

boundaries.reason: The interval [0,S_*] and the vectors X0, W0 are nonempty fixed data.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1 verifies the solution at the initial point S = 0, where X_*(0) = X0 and W_*(0) = W0; the zero-velocity case W0 = 0 gives the standing oscillation cos(LS)X0 by the same formula.

boundaries.reason: The scaled system is three-dimensional; no one-dimensional specialization is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: step 3.1 bounds |X_*(S)| ≤ |X0| + |W0|/L independently of the relative size of X0 and W0, so the degenerate case of small amplitude or slow oscillation is covered without a separate branch; the ball is nondegenerate whenever S_* > 0.
step 3.1 takes the supremum over the closed interval [0,S_*] and step 4.1 states the bound on the same closed interval, covering both endpoints.

boundaries.reason: The data X0, W0 and S_* are fixed; no selection occurs.
The example verifies hypotheses for an explicit solution; no equivalence is asserted.
No converse (for example that only harmonic data satisfy the hypotheses) is claimed.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h$ on $\Omega$ with components $h_{ab}$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) — the **first-order
perturbation** — and a smooth family $q$ of symmetric component fields
$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
and $p\in\Omega$, such that for every $\lambda$ with
$0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\lambda)$ on
$\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $q$ is the **normalized remainder**. The
family is thus normalized so that $g(0)=\eta$ is its value at
$\lambda=0$ and $h=\partial_\lambda g(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}$. No assumption
is made that $g(\lambda)$ solves any field equation; the metrics $g(\lambda)$
are the mathematical input of the linearization.

**(b) First-order coefficients.** Let $A(\lambda)$ stand for any of the
component families $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))$, $S(g(\lambda))$,
$G_{ab}(g(\lambda))$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\lambda)$; these
are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ because the Christoffel symbols, the curvature
components and the inverse metric are smooth functions of the metric
components and their derivatives
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Define the **first-order
coefficients**

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and
lowered with the flat metric $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{ab}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]): $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$,
$h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$, and

$$\Box:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b=-\partial_0^2+\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2$$

is the **d'Alembertian** of the flat metric, applied componentwise to
component families. The **trace** of $h$ and the **trace-reversed
perturbation** are

$$h:=\eta^{ab}h_{ab},\qquad \bar h_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,h\,\eta_{ab} .$$

The inverse passage is the same formula, $\bar h_{ab}$'s trace being
$\eta^{ab}\bar h_{ab}=h-2h=-h$: explicitly

$$h_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\eta^{cd}\bar h_{cd} .$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For a smooth covector field $\xi_b$ on
$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.

Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be an open set of the flat model
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], let
$(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over $\Omega$ with
first-order coefficients $\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}$, $S^{(1)}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}$ and with trace
reversal $\bar h$, d'Alembertian $\Box$ and gauge transformation
$h'_{ab}=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ as in
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]], and let $L>0$ be a length scale.
All components are taken in the inertial chart and all contractions are
with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$.

**(a) Christoffel symbols.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there is a
constant $C_K<\infty$ such that for all $p\in K$ and
$0<|\lambda|\le\varepsilon_1/2$,

$$\Bigl|\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,\eta^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bh_{cd}+\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(b) Ricci tensor.** With the same constants (enlarged if necessary),

$$\Bigl|\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_c\partial_a h^{c}{}_{b}+\partial_c\partial_b h^{c}{}_{a}-\Box h_{ab}-\partial_a\partial_b h\bigr).$$

**(c) Scalar curvature and Einstein tensor.** With the same constants,

$$\Bigl|S(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,S^{(1)}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad S^{(1)}=\partial_a\partial_bh^{ab}-\Box h,$$

and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,G^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h_{ab}+\partial^c\partial_{(a}\bar h_{b)c}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}.$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on
$\Omega$,

$$\bar h'{}_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a+\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\xi_c,\qquad \partial^a\bar h'{}_{ab}=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}-\Box\xi_b .$$

Consequently $h'$ is in harmonic gauge exactly when
$\Box\xi_b=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}$, and in that case

$$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h'{}_{ab}.$$

**(e) Gauge invariance of the first-order curvature.** For every smooth
covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,

$$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h),\qquad S^{(1)}(h')=S^{(1)}(h),\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=G^{(1)}_{ab}(h).$$

That is, subtracting the pure-gauge perturbation
$\partial_a\xi_b+\partial_b\xi_a$ from the first-order perturbation leaves
the first-order Ricci, scalar and Einstein tensors unchanged; their
first-order coefficients depend on $h$ only through its gauge-equivalence
class.

**(f) Quadratic remainder.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there are
$\delta_0>0$ and $C_K<\infty$ such that for every smooth symmetric component
field $A=(A_{ab})$ on a neighborhood of $K$ with

$$B_K(A):=\sup_K\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|+L^{-1}\sup_K\max_{a,b,c}|\partial_cA_{ab}|+L^{-2}\sup_K\max_{a,b,c,d}|\partial_c\partial_dA_{ab}|\le\delta_0,$$

the metric $\eta+A$ is Lorentzian of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $K$ and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+A)(p)-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)(p)\Bigr|\le \frac{C_K\,B_K(A)^2}{L^2}\qquad(p\in K),$$

where $G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)$ is the right-hand side of the displayed formula of
(c) with $h$ replaced by $A$, and $G_{ab}(\eta+A)$ is the Einstein tensor of
the metric with components $\eta_{ab}+A_{ab}$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), so that at every $p\in M$ the form
$g_p$ has inertia $(3,1,0)$, and let $h$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on $M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) whose
support is compact.

**(a) Pointwise openness.** Let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $4$
and let $G$ be a symmetric bilinear form on $V$ of inertia $(3,1,0)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). If in some basis of $V$ the matrix of $G$
has the form $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)+E$, then $G$ has inertia $(3,1,0)$
whenever $|E_{ij}|<1/8$ for all $i,j$. Consequently, for every basis the set
of matrices of symmetric forms of inertia $(3,1,0)$ is open in the space
$M_4^{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbb R)$ with respect to the maximum-entry norm, and
equivalently $g_p$ has a neighborhood in the space of symmetric forms at $p$
consisting entirely of forms of inertia $(3,1,0)$.

**(b) Global stability.** There is $\lambda_0>0$ such that for every real
$\lambda$ with $|\lambda|<\lambda_0$ the smooth symmetric field $g+\lambda h$
is a smooth Lorentzian metric on $M$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, with
time orientation inherited from $N$ (the field $N$ remains timelike for
$g+\lambda h$ for $|\lambda|$ small).

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
