space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: (The family.) The fields $h$ and $q\equiv0$ are smooth and stationary, and for $0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1=1/4$ and $p\in\Omega$ the matrix of $g(\lambda)$ in the coordinate frame is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)+E$ with $E_{ab}=\lambda h_{ab}$, so $|E_{ab}|\le2|\lambda|\cdot\sup_\Omega|\varphi|<1/2<1/8$ by [L6]; hence by [L5] each $g(\lambda)$ is a smooth Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $\Omega$ and $(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ is a flat linearized family.

(First-order vacuum.) By [L1], $h=\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=2\varphi-6\varphi=-4\varphi$, so $\bar h_{00}=-2\varphi-\frac12(-1)(-4\varphi)=-4\varphi$ and $\bar h_{0i}=0$, $\bar h_{ij}=-2\varphi\delta_{ij}-\frac12\delta_{ij}(-4\varphi)=0$; that is, $\bar h_{ab}=-4\varphi\,\delta_{a0}\delta_{b0}$. With $\Box\varphi=\Delta\varphi=0$ and stationarity, the closed formula of [L2] gives $G^{(1)}_{00}=-\frac12\Box(-4\varphi)=2\Delta\varphi=0$, while $\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}=\eta^{00}\eta^{00}\partial_0\partial_0\bar h_{00}=0$ and every divergence term involves $\bar h_{0\cdot}$ components or time derivatives; the $(0i)$ and $(ij)$ components contain only such terms as well. Hence $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)=0$; by the linearity of [L2], $G^{(1)}_{ab}(\lambda h)=\lambda G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)=0$ for every $\lambda$.

(Exact Christoffel symbols.) In the coordinate frame $g(\lambda)=\operatorname{diag}(-p,q,q,q)$, so $g^{00}=-1/p$ and $g^{ii}=1/q$; the general formula of [L3] and [L6] give, and all other components vanish: $\Gamma^0{}_{01}=\Gamma^0{}_{10}=\partial_1p/(2p)=\lambda/p$; $\Gamma^1{}_{00}=\partial_1p/(2q)=\lambda/q$; $\Gamma^1{}_{11}=\partial_1q/(2q)=-\lambda/q$; $\Gamma^1{}_{22}=\Gamma^1{}_{33}=-\partial_1q/(2q)=\lambda/q$; $\Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^2{}_{21}=\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\Gamma^3{}_{31}=\partial_1q/(2q)=-\lambda/q$. (For example $\Gamma^1{}_{22}=\frac12g^{11}(\partial_2g_{12}+\partial_2g_{21}-\partial_1g_{22})=\frac12(1/q)(-\partial_1q)$, since only the $\partial_1$ derivative of the diagonal entries is nonzero; all components with a time derivative vanish by stationarity.)

(Exact Ricci component.) By [L3] and step 1.3, $R^{a}{}_{0a0}=\partial_a\Gamma^a{}_{00}-\partial_0\Gamma^a{}_{a0}+\Gamma^a{}_{ae}\Gamma^e{}_{00}-\Gamma^a{}_{0e}\Gamma^e{}_{a0}$ and $\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=R^{a}{}_{0a0}$. The terms are: $\partial_a\Gamma^a{}_{00}=\partial_1(\lambda/q)=2\lambda^2/q^2$ by [L6]; $\partial_0\Gamma^a{}_{a0}=0$; $\Gamma^a{}_{a1}=\Gamma^0{}_{01}+\Gamma^1{}_{11}+\Gamma^2{}_{21}+\Gamma^3{}_{31}=\lambda/p-3\lambda/q$, so $\Gamma^a{}_{ae}\Gamma^e{}_{00}=\Gamma^a{}_{a1}\Gamma^1{}_{00}=\lambda^2/(pq)-3\lambda^2/q^2$; and $\Gamma^a{}_{0e}\Gamma^e{}_{a0}=\Gamma^0{}_{01}\Gamma^1{}_{00}+\Gamma^1{}_{00}\Gamma^0{}_{10}=2\lambda^2/(pq)$. Summing, $\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=2\lambda^2/q^2+\lambda^2/(pq)-3\lambda^2/q^2-2\lambda^2/(pq)=-\lambda^2/q^2-\lambda^2/(pq)=-\lambda^2(p+q)/(pq^2)=-2\lambda^2/(pq^2)$ since $p+q=2$ by [L6].

(Refutation.) At the origin $x=0$ one has $p=q=1$, so step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{Ric}_{00}(g(\lambda))= -2\lambda^2
eq0$ for every $0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$; hence the exact Ricci tensor does not vanish on $\Omega$. If the exact Einstein tensor vanished, then contracting $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}- rac12Sg_{ab}$ of [L3] with $g^{ab}$ would give $S=-g^{ab}G_{ab}=0$ and then $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=G_{ab}+ rac12Sg_{ab}=0$, contradicting $\operatorname{Ric}_{00}
eq0$. So $G_{ab}(g(\lambda))
eq0$ on $\Omega$ although $G^{(1)}_{ab}(\lambda h)=0$ by step 1.2, which refutes the statement. The failure is of order $\lambda^2$, consistent with the quadratic remainder bound of [[thm-gr-flat-linearized-curvature-and-gauge]] clause (f).

boundaries.reason: Ω is the nonempty unit ball and the family is defined for 0 < |λ| < 1/4; no empty set arises.

boundaries.evidence: step 3.1 evaluates Ric_00 at the origin and finds -2λ², and step 2.1 removes every term of G^(1) precisely because Δφ = 0, which is the zero case of the first-order coefficient; the refutation rests on the vanishing first-order and nonvanishing second-order terms.

boundaries.reason: The computation is four-dimensional; no one-dimensional case is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 keeps |Lh_ab| ≤ 2|λ| < 1/2 so each g(λ) is Lorentzian; the degenerate values of λ at which p or q would vanish are excluded by the explicit range.

boundaries.reason: The evaluation is at the interior point x = 0 and on the open ball; no interval endpoint is asserted.
The perturbation and the evaluation point are explicitly fixed.
The counterexample refutes one implication; it asserts no equivalence.
The converse implication is neither claimed nor used.

citations.quote:
Let $M:=\mathbb R^4$ carry its standard smooth structure
([[def-smooth-manifold]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ be the **identity chart**, $x(p)=p$;
it is a global chart of the maximal smooth atlas, and the coordinate
derivations $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3$ form a basis of
$T_pM$ at every $p\in M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). Write

$$\eta:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$$

for the standard Lorentz form of inertia $(3,1,0)$ in this basis
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

**(a) The metric.** Define the covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ on $M$ by the
requirement that its components in the identity chart are the constants

$$g_{ab}:=\eta_{ab}\qquad(a,b=0,1,2,3),$$

that is, $g_p(\partial_a|_p,\partial_b|_p)=\eta_{ab}$ for every $p\in M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]] clause (a)). The component
functions are constant, hence $C^\infty$, so $g$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field; at every $p$ the form $g_p$ is nondegenerate with
inertia $(3,1,0)$. By [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a) the
pair $(M,g)$ is therefore a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$.

**(b) The inertial chart and frame.** The chart $x$ is called the **inertial
chart** of the flat model. In this chart the coordinate frame
$(\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3)$ is a $g$-orthonormal frame at
every point, $g(\partial_a,\partial_b)=\eta_{ab}$; it is simultaneously a
coordinate frame and a **tetrad field** in the sense of
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]], defined on all of $M$.

**(c) Time orientation and causal classification.** Define the smooth vector
field $N:=\partial_0$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). Since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)=\eta_{00}=-1<0$ for every $p$, the field $N$ is everywhere
timelike, so $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). For a nonzero tangent
vector $v=v^a\partial_a|_p$ the definitions of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c) and
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] give

$$g_p(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(v^i)^2,\qquad g_p(v,N_p)=-v^0 .$$

so $v$ is **future-directed** exactly when $v^0>0$, and

- $v$ is future timelike $\iff$ $v^0>0$ and $(v^0)^2>\sum_i(v^i)^2$;
- $v$ is future null $\iff$ $v^0>0$ and $(v^0)^2=\sum_i(v^i)^2$;
- $v$ is spacelike $\iff$ $(v^0)^2<\sum_i(v^i)^2$;

consequently the future causal cone at every point is
$\{v\neq0: v^0\ge\sqrt{\sum_i(v^i)^2}\}$. These are the standard readings of
the Minkowski form in the inertial chart; the chain of equivalences is the
specialization of the causal classification to this pair $(g_p,N_p)$ and is
recorded here for later use.

**(d) Scope.** This item defines geometric data only: a manifold, a metric
field, a time orientation and a distinguished chart and frame. It makes no
claim about curvature, about any field equation, about which geometry a
physical model uses, or about nature; the physical reading of the data, the
dimensions of the coordinates and the numerical values or signs of physical
constants belong to the framework's unit conventions and postulates, which
are separate items. In particular no relation between the coordinate
functions $x^a$ and physical time or length measurements is asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with its inertial chart $x$,
and let $\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Vanishing connection.** In the inertial chart all Christoffel symbols
of $\nabla$ vanish identically:

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\equiv0\qquad(a,b,c=0,1,2,3).$$

**(b) Vanishing curvature.** The curvature operator of $\nabla$ vanishes
identically, $R\equiv0$; consequently the curvature components, the Ricci
tensor, the scalar curvature and the Einstein tensor vanish identically,

$$R^a{}_{bcd}\equiv0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ab}\equiv0,\qquad S\equiv0,\qquad G_{ab}\equiv0 .$$

**(c) Translation Killing fields.** Each coordinate field $\partial_a$ is a
Killing field of $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-killing-field]]); in particular the time
orientation field $N=\partial_0$ is a unit timelike Killing field.

**(d) Straight geodesics.** A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ on an interval
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]) is a geodesic of $\nabla$ if and
only if there are $x_0,v\in\mathbb R^4$ such that

$$x\bigl(\gamma(s)\bigr)=x_0+s\,v\qquad(s\in I).$$

For such a geodesic the speed is constant,
$g(\gamma',\gamma')=\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(v^i)^2$; the maximal
geodesic with $x(\gamma(0))=x_0$ and $x(\gamma)'(0)=v$ has domain
$\mathbb R$. If $\eta(v,v)<0$ and $v^0>0$, the geodesic is a future timelike
worldline
([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]) and the parameter
$\tau(s):=\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}\,(s-s_0)/c$ is proper time up to an additive
constant, with $d\gamma/d\tau$ the physical four-velocity
$U$, $g(U,U)=-c^2$
([[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]] clause 3).

**(e) Inertial-chart velocity reading.** Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic as in
(d) with $\eta(v,v)<0$, $v^0>0$, written in the inertial chart as
$x(\gamma(t))=(ct,\mathbf q(t))$ with $\mathbf q$ the spatial part and $t$
the parameter $t=x^0/c$. Then the coordinate velocity
$\mathbf w:=d\mathbf q/dt$ is the constant vector
$(cv^1,v^0,\dots)$-reading $\mathbf w=(c/v^0)(v^1,v^2,v^3)$, and
$|\mathbf w|<c$.

Let $(\hat M,\hat g)$ be a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), let $\Gamma$ be a discrete
group equipped with its discrete smooth structure (a zero-dimensional Lie
group, so that a **smooth action** is one for which every map
$p\mapsto\gamma\cdot p$, $\gamma\in\Gamma$, is smooth), and let $\Gamma$ act
on $\hat M$ smoothly, freely and properly in the sense of
[[def-free-and-proper-lie-group-actions]]; write $\gamma\cdot p$ for the
action and $d\gamma_p$ for the differential of $p\mapsto\gamma\cdot p$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]). Suppose that every $\gamma\in\Gamma$
**preserves $\hat g$**, that is
$$\hat g_{\gamma\cdot p}\bigl(d\gamma_p V,d\gamma_p W\bigr)=\hat g_p(V,W)$$
for all $p\in\hat M$, $V,W\in T_p\hat M$ and $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Let
$q:\hat M\to M:=\hat M/\Gamma$ be the orbit map. Then:

**(a)** $M$ is a Hausdorff second-countable smooth four-manifold, $q$ is a
smooth surjective submersion, and $q$ is a local diffeomorphism at every
point of $\hat M$.

**(b)** There is a unique smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ on $M$ with $q^*g=\hat g$; equivalently
$g_{q(p)}(dq_pV,dq_pW)=\hat g_p(V,W)$ for all $p,V,W$.

**(c)** If $\hat N$ is a smooth vector field on $\hat M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) which is
$\Gamma$-invariant, $\hat N_{\gamma\cdot p}=d\gamma_p(\hat N_p)$, and
satisfies $\hat g(\hat N,\hat N)<0$, then the prescription
$N_{q(p)}:=dq_p(\hat N_p)$ defines a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$ with
$g(N,N)<0$ for all points. In particular, a $\Gamma$-invariant time
orientation of $(\hat M,\hat g)$ descends to one of $(M,g)$.

Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$ and let $X$ be a set. A **left action** of
$G$ on $X$ is a function $G\times X\to X$, written $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$,
such that

$$e\cdot x=x,\qquad (gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$$

for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$. Then $X$ is a **$G$-set**. The action is
**transitive** when every $x,y\in X$ satisfy $g\cdot x=y$ for some $g\in G$.
It is **faithful** when $g\cdot x=x$ for every $x\in X$ implies $g=e$.

A smooth action of a Lie group $G$ on a manifold $M$ is **free** if
$G_x=\{e\}$ for every $x\in M$.

It is **proper** if its action-graph map

$$\Theta:G\times M\longrightarrow M\times M,\qquad \Theta(g,x)=(g\cdot x,x),$$

is proper: $\Theta^{-1}(K)$ is compact for every compact
$K\subseteq M\times M$. The reversed coordinate convention
$(x,g\cdot x)$ is equivalent by the factor-swap homeomorphism. Freeness and
properness are independent conditions; neither is encoded by the other.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth and let $p\in M$. The **differential of $F$ at $p$** is the map $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ defined by
$$ dF_p(v)([g]):=v([g\circ F]) $$
for every derivation $v\in T_pM$ and every germ $[g]\in C_{F(p)}^\infty(N)$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as functions on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)\,g'(c) \;=\; \bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr)\,f'(c) .$$

**The statement is a product identity, and that is deliberate.** The familiar
quotient form

$$\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{g(b)-g(a)} \;=\; \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}$$

is not asserted here, and it is not equivalent: its left side needs
$g(b) \ne g(a)$ and its right side needs $g'(c) \ne 0$, and neither follows from
the hypotheses. The product form above needs neither, holds under exactly the
hypotheses stated, and specialises to the quotient form whenever both
denominators happen to be nonzero. The companion page exhibits an $f$ and a $g$
for which the quotient form is meaningless while the product form holds.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth and let $p\in M$. The **differential of $F$ at $p$** is the map $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ defined by
$$ dF_p(v)([g]):=v([g\circ F]) $$
for every derivation $v\in T_pM$ and every germ $[g]\in C_{F(p)}^\infty(N)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: (The action.) In the chart $x$ the action reads $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\mapsto(x^0+nL,x^1,x^2,x^3)$; each $p\mapsto n\cdot p$ is a smooth translation, so the action is smooth; it is an action of the group $\mathbb Z$ on $\hat M$ with $0\cdot p=p$ and $(n+m)\cdot p=n\cdot(m\cdot p)$. It is free: $n\cdot p=p$ forces $nL=0$, hence $n=0$. It preserves $\hat g$: the differential of a translation in the chart is the identity, so $\hat g_{n\cdot p}(d(n\cdot)_pV,d(n\cdot)_pW)=\hat g_p(V,W)$ by [L1]. It is proper: if $K_1,K_2\subseteq\hat M$ are compact and $p\in K_1$ with $n\cdot p\in K_2$, then $|n|L\le\sup_{K_1}|x^0|+\sup_{K_2}|x^0|<\infty$ by [L8], so only finitely many $n$ occur; hence $\Theta^{-1}(K_1\times K_2)$ is a finite union of compact sets, one for each such $n$, and is compact. Finally $\hat N=\partial_0$ is $\Gamma$-invariant with $\hat g(\hat N,\hat N)=-1<0$, since it is invariant under translations.

(The quotient and the closed curve.) By step 1.1 and [L2], applied to the discrete Lie group $\Gamma$ of [L3], $M$ is a Hausdorff second-countable smooth four-manifold, $q$ is smooth and a local diffeomorphism, there is a unique smooth Lorentzian $g$ with $q^*g=\hat g$, and $\hat N$ descends to a time orientation $N$; $M$ is connected as the image of the connected $\hat M$ under the continuous surjection $q$. The curve $\hat\sigma(s):=x^{-1}(s,0,0,0)$ on $[0,L]$ is smooth with $\hat\sigma(L)=(0,0,0,0)=\hat\sigma(0)+L e_0=1\cdot\hat\sigma(0)$; hence $\sigma:=q\circ\hat\sigma$ is smooth by [L5] and satisfies $\sigma(L)=q(1\cdot\hat\sigma(0))=q(\hat\sigma(0))=\sigma(0)$. Its tangent is $\sigma'(s)=dq_{\hat\sigma(s)}(\partial_0)\neq0$ by the local-diffeomorphism property, and by [L2] $g(\sigma',\sigma')=\hat g(\partial_0,\partial_0)=-1<0$; similarly $g(N,\sigma')=-1<0$, so $\sigma$ is future-directed. Thus $\sigma$ is a nonconstant closed future timelike curve.

(Flatness.) Let $r\in M$ and $p\in q^{-1}(r)$. Since $q$ is a local diffeomorphism there are open neighborhoods $\hat U$ of $p$ and $V$ of $r$ with $q|_{\hat U}:\hat U\to V$ a diffeomorphism; let $s:V\to\hat U$ be its inverse and $u:=x\circ s:V\to\mathbb R^4$ the induced chart ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). For $r'\in V$ and $v,w\in T_{r'}M$ one has $g_{r'}(v,w)=\hat g_{s(r')}(ds_{r'}v,ds_{r'}w)$ by $q^*g=\hat g$ from [L2]; in components, by [L5], $g_{ab}=\partial_au^c\partial_bu^d(\hat g_{cd}\circ s)=\eta_{ab}$, constant, because $u=x\circ s$ and $\hat g_{cd}=\eta_{cd}$ constant by [L1]. By [L6] the Christoffel symbols of the metric-selected connection vanish identically in this chart, and then the curvature formula of [L4] gives $R^a{}_{bcd}(r)=0$. As $r\in M$ was arbitrary and vanishing of a tensor at a point is chart-independent, $R\equiv0$ on $M$. The same charts exhibit for each point a neighborhood isometric to an open subset of Minkowski space, in accordance with clause (d) of [[thm-gr-vanishing-curvature-implies-locally-minkowski]].

(No global isometry.) Suppose $F:M\to\mathbb R^4$ satisfies $F^*\eta=g$. Let $f:=(F\circ\sigma)^0=x^0\circ F\circ\sigma$; $f$ is smooth by [L5], so continuous on $[0,L]$ and differentiable on $(0,L)$, with $f(L)-f(0)=0$ because $\sigma(L)=\sigma(0)$. By [L7] there is $c\in(0,L)$ with $f'(c)=0$. On the other hand, for every $s$, [L8] and step 2.1 give $\eta\bigl((F\circ\sigma)'(s),(F\circ\sigma)'(s)\bigr)=g(\sigma'(s),\sigma'(s))=-1$, that is
$$-\bigl(f'(s)\bigr)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3\bigl((F\circ\sigma)^i\bigr)'(s)^2=-1,$$
so $\bigl(f'(s)\bigr)^2=1+\sum_{i=1}^3((F\circ\sigma)^i)'(s)^2\ge1$ and $f'(s)\neq0$; in particular $f'(c)\neq0$, a contradiction. Hence no such $F$ exists. Since a global chart $u$ with $g_{ab}=\eta_{ab}$ constant would make $u$ an isometry onto its image (with $\eta$ given by those constants), no such chart exists either.

(Conclusion.) Steps 2.1 and 3.1 produce a connected time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ with $R\equiv0$ and a nonconstant closed future timelike curve; step 3.2 shows it is not isometric to Minkowski space and admits no global chart with constant components $\eta_{ab}$. This refutes the statement; the local isometry statement of [[thm-gr-vanishing-curvature-implies-locally-minkowski]] is not contradicted but is precisely local, as its clause (d) asserts. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎



- **Local versus global.** The example isolates the topological obstruction to the converse of the local flatness theorem: vanishing curvature gives locally constant-component charts but does not prevent a compact timelike direction, which produces closed timelike curves and defeats the global argument in step 3.2 (the real-valued function $f$ on the circle direction cannot be strictly increasing). The construction is purely mathematical: no matter, observer, clock or measurement occurs.
- **Related models.** Other identification patterns of the flat model give flat manifolds with different global properties (for example identifications by spacelike translations, as in the flat torus). The specific timelike identification here is the one for which the closed curve is timelike; a spacelike identification instead yields closed spacelike curves and no closed causal curve.
